title: EPA seeks to eliminate remaining greenhouse-gas rules for power plants
gist: The EPA finalized a rule gutting the Biden-era 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards for power plants and simultaneously proposed revoking all remaining greenhouse gas requirements for the power sector, claiming power plant emissions 'have no material impact on climate change.' Combined with February's repeal of the motor-vehicle endangerment finding, this completes the rollback of federal climate regulation on both the power and transportation sectors — the two largest US emissions sources — and sets up litigation over whether a 'non-endangerment finding' can survive the 2007 Supreme Court ruling and 2009 endangerment finding.

insights.claim: The EPA announced a final plan on Monday that guts the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, asserting the rule exceeded its Clean Air Act authority by requiring control technologies that are 'not adequately demonstrated.'
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Removes the forced-retirement clock on coal and unabated gas generation, extending economic life for merchant thermal assets and reducing near-term CCS capex obligations.
insights.locator: The Environmental Protection Agency announced a final plan Monday

insights.claim: Beyond repealing the 2024 standards, the EPA separately proposed revoking all remaining greenhouse gas emissions requirements for power plants, arguing those emissions 'have no material impact on climate change.'
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: A full revocation, not a weakening — the regulatory floor for US power-sector carbon goes to zero, shifting all decarbonization pressure onto state mandates and corporate PPAs.
insights.quote: all remaining GHG emissions requirements for power plants
insights.locator: The agency also proposed revoking

insights.claim: Power plants are the second-largest source of US greenhouse gas emissions, behind transportation, and the Trump administration has now removed federal climate regulation from both.
insights.speaker: Zealan Hoover
insights.so_what: With both top emitting sectors deregulated federally, US emissions trajectory becomes a function of economics and state policy alone — repricing carbon-intensive assets upward and clean-energy tax equity demand downward.
insights.quote: And with today’s regulatory rollback, the Trump administration has now finished its work to end the climate regulations on both.
insights.locator: The two largest sources of climate emissions in the United States

insights.claim: The plan to revoke the Carbon Pollution Standards was first revealed in spring 2026, meaning the market had roughly two quarters of advance notice before finalization.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Much of the repeal is likely already in thermal generator valuations; the incremental news is the total revocation proposal, not the repeal itself.
insights.locator: The plan to revoke the Carbon Pollution Standards was initially revealed last spring.

themes.theme: The endangerment finding as legal keystone

insights.claim: The Supreme Court ruled in 2007 that the Clean Air Act's definition of air pollutants includes greenhouse gases and that the EPA must act to reduce them if it finds they endanger health and the environment; the EPA made that endangerment finding in 2009.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: The entire federal climate-regulation edifice rests on one administrative finding — which is why attacking it, not individual rules, is the high-leverage move for both sides.
insights.locator: In 2007, the Supreme Court ruled that the Clean Air Act's definition of air pollutants

insights.claim: A former senior EPA advisor argues the administration is attacking the entire legal framework for climate regulation by asserting climate pollution does not harm human health or welfare, rather than merely relaxing individual standards.
insights.speaker: Zealan Hoover
insights.so_what: If the endangerment predicate falls, no future EPA can re-regulate GHGs without fresh litigation or new legislation — a structurally longer deregulated runway than a typical policy swing.
insights.quote: The Trump administration is now kicking the legs out from under the entire legal framework for regulating climate pollution by arguing that climate pollution does not harm human health or welfare
insights.locator: said Zealan Hoover, a former senior advisor to the EPA

insights.claim: A senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity's Climate Law Institute expects the administration to issue an affirmative 'non-endangerment finding' so it has no obligation to regulate greenhouse gases at all, and predicts it will not survive judicial review.
insights.speaker: Maggie Coulter
insights.so_what: Litigation risk means the deregulation is not durable — model a probability-weighted scenario where rules are reinstated by courts rather than assuming permanent relief.
insights.quote: Will this stand up in court? We would argue, definitely not.
insights.locator: Maggie Coulter, senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity's Climate Law Institute

insights.claim: The rollback follows a three-part sequence: first repeal the endangerment finding, second roll back the regulations that relied on it, third block future efforts to regulate climate pollution.
insights.speaker: Zealan Hoover
insights.so_what: A named playbook lets investors anticipate step three — watch for procedural rulemaking that raises the bar for any future GHG regulation, the last unpriced leg.
insights.locator: Part one was repealing the endangerment finding, Hoover said.

insights.claim: Unlike the first Trump administration — whose public health repeals were largely reinstated under Biden — the current effort is deliberately designed to make re-regulation by a future administration extremely difficult.
insights.speaker: Zealan Hoover
insights.so_what: Reduces the mean-reversion assumption on US climate policy across election cycles; regulatory risk premia on fossil assets should compress more than a single-term rollback would justify.
insights.quote: but burning them to the ground
insights.locator: The first Trump administration repealed a bunch of public health regulations

insights.claim: Trump's EPA claims the new power plant rule will save $310 billion by unleashing coal and natural gas, with the separate proposal to rescind every remaining GHG standard for the power sector saving an additional $370 million in direct compliance costs.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Note the three-orders-of-magnitude gap between the headline $310B and the $370M of actual direct compliance savings — the big number is not compliance cost relief.
insights.locator: In announcing the power plant regulations repeal, Trump's EPA said only that

insights.claim: Resources for the Future's cost-benefit analysis finds that elevated toxic air contaminant emissions triggered by the repeal would produce health damages costing up to $476 billion — exceeding the administration's own claimed $310 billion in savings.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: A credible counter-analysis showing net negative economics gives litigants an arbitrary-and-capricious argument and raises reversal odds on the rule.
insights.locator: elevated emissions of toxic air contaminants triggered by the repeal

insights.claim: Biden's EPA projected in June 2024 that the Carbon Pollution Standards would cut 1.38 billion metric tons of carbon through 2047 — equivalent to nearly a full year of US electric power sector emissions or the annual output of 328 million gas-powered cars.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Quantifies the emissions swing now back in play through 2047 — relevant to voluntary carbon market supply/demand and to corporates with Scope 2 targets tied to grid intensity.
insights.locator: The agency pointed to a regulatory impact analysis that projected reductions

insights.claim: The Trump administration is heavily discounting or entirely refusing to quantify public health benefits in its regulatory analyses, which breaks the cost-benefit machinery the entire federal regulatory framework is built on.
insights.speaker: Zealan Hoover
insights.so_what: Methodology changes in benefit valuation propagate across every agency rulemaking, not just climate — a systematic tailwind for regulated-industry compliance costs broadly.
insights.quote: heavily discounting, if not completely refusing
insights.locator: The entire regulatory framework is based on cost-benefit analyses, Hoover said.

insights.claim: Independent studies find that coal power is driving higher, not lower, utility costs for consumers, contradicting the administration's claim that the repeal will save families and businesses billions.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: If coal dispatch raises retail rates, deregulation does not automatically translate into consumer savings or into load growth — watch utility rate cases for the real signal.
insights.locator: Independent studies, however, have reported that coal power is driving higher utility costs

themes.theme: Parallel front: vehicles and state waivers

insights.claim: In February the EPA overturned the endangerment finding underpinning its authority to regulate greenhouse gases from motor vehicles, the largest single source of US climate pollution.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Removes the federal regulatory forcing function behind US EV adoption curves — a direct negative for EV volume assumptions and battery supply-chain demand.
insights.locator: In February, the EPA overturned the endangerment finding

insights.claim: The EPA used a parliamentary maneuver to revoke decades-old Clean Air Act waivers underpinning California's vehicle emissions standards, but a federal judge has temporarily blocked the move.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: California's waiver is the backstop that keeps a de facto national EV standard alive; the injunction's outcome determines whether automakers can abandon compliance planning.
insights.locator: the agency attacked states' rights to pass stricter climate regulations

insights.claim: The rollback was announced on the heels of the hottest summer on record and a UN report warning global temperatures are likely to push climate risks to 'increasingly dangerous heights.'
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Policy and physical climate signals are now actively diverging — physical risk repricing in insurance and real assets will proceed independently of US regulation.
insights.locator: On the heels of the hottest summer on record

insights.claim: President Trump described climate change as the 'greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world' in a United Nations speech the prior year, framing the administration's position as outright denial rather than cost-based deregulation.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Denial framing, versus a cost-benefit framing, makes the rules harder to defend in court and signals no negotiated middle ground for industry compliance planning.
insights.quote: greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world
insights.locator: President Donald Trump called climate change

insights.claim: A climate accountability researcher argues the US government has taken over the role fossil fuel companies historically played in denying climate science, removing the need for industry-funded denial campaigns.
insights.speaker: Geoffrey Supran
insights.so_what: Shifts climate-litigation targeting from corporates toward government action — potentially reducing near-term legal liability overhang on oil majors.
insights.quote: Who needs Big Oil to deny climate science, undermine science-based decision-making, and endanger people’s lives and livelihoods when the US government will do it for them?
insights.locator: asked Geoffrey Supran, director of the Climate Accountability Lab

insights.claim: An Oxford climate litigation scholar predicts that physical damages from heat waves, fires, superstorms and floods will keep accumulating regardless of regulatory posture, and that calls for accountability will only increase.
insights.speaker: Ben Franta
insights.so_what: Deregulation does not remove liability exposure — it may defer and concentrate it; watch climate litigation as the transmission channel that regulation no longer provides.
insights.quote: The government can choose to deny reality
insights.locator: said Ben Franta, an associate professor of climate litigation

insights.claim: EPA spokespersons did not respond to a request for comment on what science supports the claim that greenhouse gas emissions do not contribute significantly to dangerous air pollution.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: An unsupported scientific record is the most common ground for vacatur under the Administrative Procedure Act — a concrete marker of the rule's legal fragility.
insights.locator: EPA spokespersons did not respond to a request for comment
